prompt: why is the median so underrated

I teach 8th grade math and every year someone asks me why a negative times a negative is positive. I give the usual answers (patterns, number line flips, debt metaphors) and I can see in their faces that none of them land. Can you write an essay that actually tries to answer the question honestly, including admitting where the answer is "because we chose it that way and here's why that choice was forced on us"? Aim it at smart adults, not kids, I want to understand it better myself.
Write a short essay arguing that the birthday paradox isn't really a paradox, it's a lesson about how badly we count pairs.

My doctor told me a test I took has a 95% accuracy rate and came back positive, and I spent a week convinced I was sick before learning the condition affects like 1 in 2,000 people. I'm fine. But I'm still angry nobody explained base rates to me. Write something exploring why this mistake is so universal, even among doctors, and what it would take to make people actually feel the math instead of just being told it.
Op-ed: "Stop teaching calculus to every high schooler, teach statistics instead." Make the strongest version of that case, but don't pretend there's no cost.
What does it actually mean when the weather app says 40% chance of rain? Write it up as an essay, I feel like most explanations I've seen are confidently wrong.
essay idea: regression to the mean explains a shocking amount of folk wisdom (sophomore slumps, the Sports Illustrated cover jinx, 'punishment works better than praise'). develop it

I've been a quant at a mid-size fund for nine years. I'd like a personal-essay-style piece, first person but not about me specifically, on the quiet humiliation of discovering that most of your backtested edges were just noise. The p-hacking stuff is well known; I'm more interested in the psychology of it, what it does to your sense of your own judgment.
Why don't tipping norms ever go down? Write an essay trying to figure this out.

I'd love a short essay arguing that parking minimums are one of the most consequential and least discussed policies in American cities. I live in Columbus and half our downtown is surface lots, so feel free to use that as an example if it helps.
Write a contrarian piece: the penny should NOT be abolished (or, now that it basically has been in the US, that we lost something). I don't totally believe it but I want to see the best argument.

My dad ran a small hardware store for 30 years and always said the big box stores didn't kill him, the property tax reassessment did. I've never known if that was true or just something he told himself. Can you write an essay about how local taxes shape which small businesses survive, with his story as a frame? Doesn't have to vindicate him.
Why are concert tickets priced below what people will pay, then resold at 4x? Explain it like an essay, not an econ textbook. I want to understand why artists put up with it.
A thoughtful essay on why 'just build more housing' is correct and also why it feels like a lie to people who've watched new construction in their neighborhood and seen rents keep going up.
what I wish I knew about inflation before I started grocery shopping for a family of five. blog post style, honest, a little funny
Write an essay on the economics of the 'free' office coffee, and what it reveals about how firms think about perks versus wages.
Why does ice float, and why is that the strangest fact about ordinary life? I want an essay, not a chemistry lesson. 800 words or so.

ok so I've noticed my bread goes stale faster in the fridge than on the counter, which seems backwards. turns out it's a real thing (starch retrogradation?). could you write something exploring that, and more broadly how our intuition that 'cold = preserved' leads us astray in the kitchen
Write me an essay about why a hot shower feels so much better than a hot bath of the same temperature, or whether it even does.

Personal essay prompt: I'm a retired HVAC tech. For 40 years customers asked me why their house felt cold at 70 degrees in winter but fine at 70 in summer. The answer is radiant heat and humidity, but I always felt the real answer was that people don't understand that we sense heat flow, not temperature. Write an essay in my voice developing that idea. Plainspoken, no jargon unless I'd explain it.
Why does a song you hear once get stuck in your head for three days? Essay please
Make the case that the humble zipper is a more impressive piece of engineering than most things we call high-tech.

I'm writing for our neighborhood newsletter and want a ~1000 word piece on why everyone should learn to patch drywall. Not a how-to exactly, more an argument that small repair skills change how you relate to your house. Our readers are mostly first-time owners in 1950s ranches.

Is it actually cheaper to fix things yourself once you count your time and the tools you'll use once? Write an honest essay. I suspect the answer is 'usually no, and that's not the point' but I'd like to see it reasoned through.
essay: the case against the open-plan kitchen

We bought a 1920s house last spring and I've become slightly obsessed with how the original builders did things: plaster on wood lath, single-pane wavy glass windows, a coal chute. Every contractor who comes through wants to rip it all out and "bring it up to code". Write something exploring when old is actually better and when that's just nostalgia, without being preachy about it either way.
Why does everyone have a junk drawer? Write a playful but genuinely thoughtful essay about it.

Write an essay about learning to sharpen kitchen knives as an adult, and what it taught you about patience. I know you don't have hands, just write it as if from a home cook who finally figured it out after ruining two cheap knives.
thesis: most home maintenance disasters (rot, mold, foundation cracks) come down to water going somewhere you didn't notice. turn that into a short essay a new homeowner would actually read

Write a piece in the style of a reflective blog post on why measuring twice and cutting once is good advice that almost nobody follows, and what that says about how we actually learn practical skills.
